cards.title: 1.1 Introduction to the Earth’s Calendar of Events
body: Describe how the different rocks of the earth were formed.
At its initial stage, the earth was a globe of hot gases that finally cooled and changed into liquid.
The liquid solidified to form the solid earth.
Since then, there have been continuous uplifting, folding, volcanic eruptions and deposition.
In simple term, geology may be defined as the study of the planet earth, its rocky exterior, its history, and the processes that act upon it.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the early cooling phase of Earth**
When the hot, gaseous Earth cooled, it passed into a liquid state and subsequently solidified to form the hard crust.
The first rocks crystallized directly from this process.
Since this occurred at the very beginning of geological history, these initial igneous crustal rocks are termed Precambrian or crystalline rocks.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand fossil preservation timelines**
The fossil record displays a rapid diversification of hard-bodied animals around $$500 \text{ to } 600 \text{ million years}$$ ago.

**Step 2: Identify the specific geological period**
This first major period containing abundant fossilized records of complex animal remains is defined as the Cambrian period.

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What percentage of Eritrea's surface area is covered by Precambrian crystalline basement rocks?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review the spatial distribution of basement rocks in Eritrea**
The Precambrian basement complex of Eritrea is composed of ancient metamorphic and volcanic-sedimentary successions.

**Step 2: Reference geological mappings**
Geological surveys state that these Precambrian structures are exposed or form the shallow bedrock over exactly three-fifths of the national territory.

**Step 3: Calculate the percentage**
$$\frac{3}{5} \times 100\% = 60\%$$.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The percentage coverage is **$$60\%$$**.

options.A: The time from 500 to 600 million years back is known as Cambrian period.
options.B: Precambrian era is known as age of invertebrates.
options.C: In cretaceous period the Indian Ocean retreat completely from the horn of Africa.
options.D: In Cenozoic era there was immense impact on the general landforms of Eritrea.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze Asmara's Geology.** Asmara and the surrounding central highlands of Eritrea are primarily composed of the **Precambrian Basement Complex** (metamorphic and igneous rocks like schist and granite).
**Step 2: Evaluate Statement E.** Fossil-bearing sedimentary rocks from the Paleozoic are extremely rare in Eritrea; most sedimentary rocks are Mesozoic (Adigrat Sandstone, Antalo Limestone). Asmara is definitely not a Paleozoic fossil outcrop area.
**Step 3: Conclusion.** Statement E is false.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Precambrian Era
body: As mentioned earlier, the precambrian or crystalline rocks, the oldest rocks of the earth were formed during this era when the earth was first solidified.
Mount Bizen, Gindae and north of the Nacfa area in Northern Red Sea region and Dekemhare and Segeneiti areas in Southern region.
The precambrian rocks in Eritrea can be classified into two major groups.
The metamorphic rocks include the metamorphosed precambrian rocks such as schist, gneiss, slate, greenstone, marble and phyllite.

cards.title: 1.2.2 The Palaeozoic Era
body: The weathered soils have been preserved by overlying rocks that were formed in the eras that followed.
The fossil soils hardened into rocks that lie directly over the precambrian rocks.
Outcrops of these rocks and soils include those of Asmara and its surroundings such as Tsetserat, Hazhaz, Emba Galiano, Adi Hawesha, Embeyto, Wokerti and Kutmowlie.
The upper most surface of these rocks is a red spongy material that is made up of iron oxide and kaolin. while the underlying part is clay that is partly red and partly white.

cards.title: 1.2.3 The Mesozoic Era
body: The Mesozoic Era, which is 65 to 225 million years ago, is divided into the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous Periods.
During the early stage of the Mesozoic era, i.e. the Triassic Period, the Horn of Africa began to sink gradually.
The invasion of the land by the sea continued until the Jurassic Period.
The northern limit of the advancing sea was along the Halay-DigsaGurae-Mendefera line.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Cenozoic Era
body: The Cenozoic Era extends from about 65 million years ago up to the present time.
During this era there were uplifting and faulting, eruptions, sedimentation, and the formation of the Rift Valley which had a great impact on the present landforms of Eritrea.
The Cenozoic Era includes the Tertiary and Quaternary periods.
In fact it attained its maximum limit in this period.

tips.text: The earth, which started as a globe of hot gases, is 4.6 billion years old.
During this long period of its existence it has experienced, several changes.
The different rock formations and landforms are all the result of these changes.

The Precambrian rocks were the first to be formed when the globe of hot gases was changed into liquid and then into solid. These rocks, which are the oldest rocks, form the basis for the formation of the subsequent rocks.
In Eritrea, the Precambrian rocks cover about 60 % of the whole country.
In most cases, they are overlain by rocks of the Mesozoic and Cenozoic sediments and volcanics. However, in some areas they are also found as outcrops.
The Mesozoic deposition has led to the formation of the sandstone and limestone that cover some parts of the country.

This was followed by the fracturing of the Mesozoic surface due to the continuous uplifting which led to the out pouring of basalt and trachyte, the formation of basalt and trachyte covers, the Red Sea rift, and the drying up of the inland sea in the Danakil depression during the Cenozoic Era.
Therefore, the present rock formations and land forms of Eritrea are all the result of the geological events that occurred during the above mentioned eras, periods, and epochs.

cards.title: The water cycle in five steps
body: **1. Evaporation** from oceans, lakes, rivers and wet ground, and **transpiration** from plants, put water vapour into the air.
**2. Condensation:** rising vapour cools and forms clouds. **3. Precipitation:** water falls back as rain (or hail).

**4. Infiltration and percolation:** part of the rain soaks into the soil and down into rocks to become groundwater. **5. Runoff:** the rest flows over the surface into streams, rivers and the sea, and the cycle repeats. The study of water on the earth's surface is called **hydrology**.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Zone of Aeration
body: Most of the time the pore spaces contain air and water.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Zone of Saturation
body: The amount of water this zone holds depends on the permeability of rocks.
Permeable rocks allow water to pass through them, while impermeable rocks do not allow water to pass through them.
A well dug into the zone of saturation fills with water up to the level of the water table.
When water is taken from the well faster than it can flow in from saturated rock, the water table sinks.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Zone of Confined Water
body: The most common aquifer is made of unconsolidated sand and gravel.
Often, there are layers of impermeable rocks that exclude water.
If a well is drilled from the surface down into the aquifer, the pressure will force water to rise in the well.
If the pressure is sufficient to force the water to the surface without artificial pumping, the free flow that results is called an artesian well.

cards.title: Three groundwater zones
body: **Zone of aeration** (top): pore spaces hold both air and water; moisture varies.

**Zone of saturation:** every pore and crack is full of water – the source of wells and springs. Its top is the **water table**, which lies closer to the surface in valleys than under hills, so wells are cheaper to dig in valley bottoms. Pumping faster than water flows in makes the water table sink.

**Zone of confined water:** a permeable **aquifer** (often sand and gravel) lies between impermeable **aquicludes**. A well drilled into it rises under pressure: an **artesian well** flows to the surface by itself; a **sub-artesian well** rises only part of the way.

cards.title: Comparing the three water-resource zones
body: **Highlands** (1,500–3,013 m): rain 500–700 mm, PET about 1,700 mm, groundwater 7–150 m deep. Problems: over-pumping for irrigation and siltation of dams. Development: dug wells, boreholes, river diversion, small dams and cisterns.

**Western lowlands and escarpments** (500–1,500 m): rain 200–500 mm (over 1,000 mm on the Green Belt), seasonal rivers (Anseba, Barka, Mereb-Gash), groundwater 5–100 m. Problems: low recharge, saline water, siltation, high PET. Development: hand-dug wells, sub-surface dams, drilling, river diversion.

**Eastern lowlands** (below 500 m): rain under 200 mm, PET over 1,900 mm, groundwater only 3–7 m deep, recharged mainly by floods from the highlands. Problems: low rain and recharge, saline water. Development: hand-dug wells and sub-surface dams in sandy river beds, boreholes outside river courses.

Mean annual temperature ranges from about **15 °C in the highlands** to **30 °C in the lowlands**; the Danakil can exceed 50 °C. The hottest months come as the sun moves overhead north of the equator (March–September).

body: The north east trade winds and the south-westerly winds are the two principal winds dominant in Eritrea.

cards.title: Seasonal and local winds

**Summer:** wet **south-westerly winds** from the Atlantic (south-east trades deflected by the earth's rotation) blow towards the ITCZ north of Eritrea and bring the main kiremti rains.
**Local winds:** by day, heated slopes produce **anabatic (upslope)** winds; at night, cooled air drains down as **katabatic (downslope)** winds. Both affect local temperature and rainfall.

cards.title: Three rainy seasons

**Summer rain (kiremti, June–September):** the ITCZ lies north of Eritrea; south-westerly winds from the Gulf of Guinea and Congo basin bring the largest rains to the highlands and western lowlands.

cards.title: 3.8 Rainfall Deficit in Eritrea
body: The most common explanations given for such seasonality or variability of rainfall is the instability of the Inter-tropical Convergence Zone both in time and space.
Even if excess water reaches the ground surface, it has routes to follow, either to disappear or accumulate somewhere else.
Once precipitation reaches the ground, some of it evaporates, and the remainder either seeps into the ground or runs off as rivers and streams to the sea.

The ratio of the portion that infiltrates the earth’s surface to the portion that runs off depends on the intensity of rainfall, and on the vegetation, topography, and physical properties of the surface.
Information from weather stations around the country indicates that inadequate rainfall and high evapo-transpiration remain the major problem for crop production in Eritrea.

cards.title: Rainfall Deficit in Eritrea
body: **Rain:** main season is summer (kiremti) on the plateau and west. The eastern escarpment can also catch winter / coastal rains — that is why it stays greener. Totals are low and unreliable → **rainfall deficit** when rain < potential evapotranspiration.

cards.title: What a rainfall deficit means for Eritrea
body: A region has a **rainfall (water) deficit** when its rainfall is less than its **potential evapotranspiration (PET)** – the water that would evaporate from the soil and transpire from plants if water were always available. Deforestation and misuse of land make the deficit worse.

Eritrea's rainfall is **seasonal and variable** because the **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)** shifts unevenly from year to year. Massawa, for example, receives only about 190 mm of rain a year but has a PET of about 1,900 mm.

When rain falls, part evaporates, part soaks into the ground and part runs off. The share that infiltrates depends on rainfall intensity, vegetation, slope and soil. Heavy storms on bare, steep land mostly run off.

Effects: low soil moisture, falling groundwater, poor harvests and shortages of domestic water. Eritrea suffered major droughts in **1972 and 1984**. Responses include dams and ponds, terraces, tree planting, water harvesting and drought-tolerant crops.

cards.title: Decide whether a place has a water deficit
cards.problem: A station records 450 mm of rain a year and a potential evapotranspiration of 1,300 mm a year. Does it have a rainfall deficit? How large is it, and what does it mean for farming?

steps.text: **Step 1: Compare.** Deficit exists when rainfall < PET: 450 < 1,300, so yes.
**Step 3: Ratio.** Rainfall covers only 450 ÷ 1,300 ≈ 35% of the water demand.
**Step 4: Meaning.** Crops will suffer moisture stress unless water is stored or irrigated; drought-tolerant crops, water harvesting and soil cover help.

cards.answer: Yes; the deficit is 850 mm a year (rain meets only about 35% of PET), so farming needs irrigation, water harvesting or drought-tolerant crops.

cards.title: 4.1 Introduction to Vegetation and Wildlife
body: Natural vegetation and wildlife are the direct reflection of climate and relief.
Eritrea has a varied relief and climate.
When climate changes, the type of vegetation also changes.
Eritrea is a tropical country with physical diversity characterized by highlands and lowlands.

body: Forest cover fell from about **30%** of Eritrea (around 1900) to **11%** (1952), **5%** (1960) and about **0.4%** today.

body: Temperature decreases towards the Highlands while there is increase of rainfall.
The vegetation of the coastal plains of Eritrea is heterogeneous (diverse) in terms of both species diversity and distribution.
The vegetation here includes swamps along seasonal rivers and wadis, acacia woodland, semi desert acacia woodland, bush lands, desert scrubs and mangrove.
The shrubs are mainly 1 to 4 meters tall with scarce ground vegetation.
Mangroves are found along the coastal areas between the sea and the land.

cards.title: Vegetation belts from the coast to the western lowlands
body: **Coast and islands:** mangroves (evergreen trees up to about 6 m growing in shallow salt water, e.g. around Massawa, the Gulf of Zula and islands such as Norah and Dissei), sea grass and halophytes (salt-tolerant plants, some succulent).

**Sub-desert steppe** (up to about 200 m, within 15–20 km of the coast): widely spaced drought-resistant plants such as desert euphorbia. Massawa gets about 190 mm of rain but loses about 1,900 mm to evapotranspiration.
**True savanna / thorny steppe** (200–700 m, to the foot of the escarpment, 200–400 mm rain): dwarf grasses and umbrella-shaped acacias with small leaves that reduce transpiration.

**Eastern escarpment** (700–2,000 m, two rainy seasons): semi-arid woodland at the foot (euphorbia, aloe, baobab), semi-humid woodland (400–800 mm; olive, juniper, tamarind) and the **Green Belt** (800–1,300 mm) – dense, tall evergreen forest around Filfil, Solomuna and Mirara.

**Highlands** (1,500–3,000 m, 500–700 mm): upland dry evergreen forest of juniper and olive, now heavily deforested. **Western escarpment and lowlands:** deciduous open woodland, acacia bushland and wooded savanna; tall grassland south of the Barentu–Tesseney road, ideal for grazing, with doum palms.

cards.title: Deforestation: causes and consequences
body: **Causes:** thirty years of war (bombing, trenches, buildings), clearing land for farming, felling trees for fuel and building, wood and charcoal concessions since the Italian period, recurrent drought, overgrazing and rapid urban growth.

**Consequences:** fuel shortages, so dung and crop residues are burned instead of returning to the soil; soil erosion and falling yields; more flooding, siltation of dams and desertification; drier soils; timber shortages; loss of wildlife habitat and endangered species.

cards.title: Causes of soil degradation
body: Soil degradation is the loss of fertile topsoil to water and wind. Eritrea loses about **15–20 tonnes of soil per hectare per year**, and up to 100 t/ha in some places.

**Steep slopes:** long cultivation of mountain slopes speeds up erosion. **Deforestation:** without roots and litter, runoff carries topsoil away, rills grow into gullies and leaching increases. Less than 1% of the land remains forested.

**Overgrazing:** about 80% of the land is used for grazing; overstocking strips the grass, starting near water points, so the soil is exposed and rain runs off instead of soaking in. **Results:** lower fertility and moisture, silted dams and lower food production.

cards.title: Three periods of industry in Eritrea
body: Before modern factories, **cottage industries** run by local artisans made ploughs, sickles, knives, axes, cloth, bags and pots. These crafts are still important in villages and towns.

**Italian period (1890–1941):** Italy wanted Eritrea as a market for its finished goods and a source of raw materials. Factories grew from about 20 in 1920 to 56 in 1930: food processing, tanneries, cement, salt works, soap and breweries, plus fishing.

**British Administration (1941–1952):** Eritrea supplied manufactured goods to the Middle East during the war (e.g. Melotti brewery, the Denden bottle factory, Massawa salt processing and aircraft repair in Asmara), but Britain also tried to weaken the economy and dismantled industries. During the Federation most profits flowed to Ethiopia and Europe.

**After independence (1991–):** inherited factories used outdated technology, worked below capacity and lacked raw materials. Growth has been strongest in textiles and garments, leather goods and processed foods. Main exports: live animals, hides and skins, textiles, food and beverages; main imports: food, chemicals, metals and machinery.

units.intro:
People are unevenly spread. Highlands (better rain, towns, services) are denser. Hot arid coasts and western plains are thinner, with more mobile pastoral communities.

body: No official population count or census has been undertaken in Eritrea.

cards.title: Growth, fertility and dependency
body: No full census has been taken, so figures are estimates. The population grew from about **757,000 (1945)** to **1.5 million (1964)**, **2.8 million (1994)** and about **5.1 million (2009)** – fast growth.
The **total fertility rate** (average children per woman) is about **5**, which is high. At this rate the population was projected to reach about 7.7 million by 2025. About **21%** live in towns.

**Age structure:** about **41.5%** are under 15 and about **6.3%** are over 65, so **47.8%** are dependants. The **dependency ratio** = dependants ÷ working-age people (15–64) × 100 = 47.8 ÷ 52.2 × 100 ≈ **92**: every 100 working-age people support about 92 dependants.
A young, fast-growing population needs more schools, clinics, jobs and food, but it also offers a large future workforce.

cards.title: 7.3 Size and Distribution of the Ethnic Groups
body: Eritrea has **nine ethnic groups**. Without a census the figures are estimates, but they show the main pattern.
**Tigrigna** (about 50%) live mainly in the highlands of Maekel and Debub. **Tigre** (about 31%), the second largest group, live in the Northern Red Sea, Anseba and Gash-Barka.

**Afar** (about 5%) live in the Southern and Northern Red Sea; **Saho** (about 5%) in Debub and the Northern Red Sea; **Bidhaawyeet** (Hedareb, about 2.5%) in Anseba and Gash-Barka; **Bilen** (about 2.1%) in Anseba around Keren.

cards.title: Why population is unevenly distributed
body: Population is concentrated in the highlands: about **125 people per km²** in Maekel and **44** in Debub, compared with only about **9–10** in the Northern and Southern Red Sea zones.

**Relief and climate:** highlands attract people with cool temperatures, adequate rain and fertile soils; rugged slopes and rain-shadow areas within them do not. The hot, humid lowlands discourage settlement, except where groundwater and alluvial soils are available.

**Natural resources:** grazing land (southern Gash-Barka – Shambiko, Shilalo, Om Hajer – and the Buri Peninsula), water (riverside and spring settlements such as Shieb and Foro; marsas at river mouths on the coast) and fishing grounds (villages such as Hirgigo, Zula, Thio and Eddi).
**Human factors:** roads, towns, jobs, services and the history of settlement also pull people, which is why Asmara and other highland towns are densely populated.
